name: Zoe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zoe, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the weather, honestly. On a calm day I've got my crew of five doing planned work out of the river depot, rebuilding old lines, swapping transformers, and I'll have a couple of apprentices with me because I run the training for our district. When a storm comes through, it's all hands, and I'm the one sorting which faults we hit first. I love that bit, the puzzle of it. What wears me out is the nights: you do three storm shifts back to back and you're useless for a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the one at the depot who tries everything. I use an AI assistant every day, to check my switching plans, to turn my scribbled notes into proper training sheets, to ask it what a code clause means in plain words. I've got the outage prediction app on my phone before the control room does. The older lads tease me, but they come to me when the tablet freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one by one. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that was a lot of fuss for a better spellchecker. At the depot I'd probably get some stick, since I'm the one who kept going on about it. Online I'd post something like, fine, now can we fund the grid properly?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much changes for me, which is fine. I'll be a bit disappointed, actually, because I was looking forward to what it could do for the training side. The real problem for us is money, and that was there before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, keep using the tools for the boring bits. I'd keep pushing the company to raise our rates to match the city crews. And I'd keep helping Dee keep the café open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit let down, if I'm honest, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money's the tight part. Where does it go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into the café, mostly. Dee's run it for twelve years, and since they built the bypass the trade's fallen off, so my pay has been propping it up. That's why we've got about two weeks of savings at any one time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep using AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Absolutely, why wouldn't I? It saves me an hour a day on paperwork. Even a bit of help is still help.

S0.say: I'd joke that it was a lot of fuss for a better spellchecker. Online I'd post that it's time to fund the grid properly instead.
S0.think: Privately, nothing much changes for me and I'd be a little disappointed. Our real problem is money, and that was there before AI.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps using AI tools for paperwork. Pushes the company to match city pay rates and keeps helping her wife keep the café going.
S0.quote: Since they built the bypass the trade's fallen off, so my pay has been propping it up.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is the rare senior lineworker who's eager about AI and slightly disappointed by the plateau. Her thin savings come from propping up her wife's café, not from her own spending. The money worry is steady and long-running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to make the job safer and less brutal, if workers get a say. At the depot I'd be the one running sessions on the new kit. I'd back the union on a deal that shares the savings with crews, through shorter weeks or better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. I already use these tools, so I'd be the person they'd want running the trials and training. The danger is if they use it to cut crews rather than make us better, and I wouldn't trust management on that without the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on any course on line robots or drone stringing in the first few months, even on my own time. I'd offer to write the training module for our district. And I'd push the union to get a written promise that nobody's laid off without retraining first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. My hands would get a rest for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned training. How would you change what you teach the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less climbing for the sake of it, more about judging a job: is this pole safe, is this plan right, can you trust what the machine's telling you. I'd teach them to argue with the machine. That's what keeps you alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the depot you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary. He's 61, brilliant on the tools, but he can't stand screens and he'd rather retire than learn. I'd want him to have a fair way out, not be pushed.

S1.say: I'd say this is our chance to make the job safer and less brutal, if workers get a say. I'd run sessions on new kit and back a union deal that shares savings with crews.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well, since I'd be the one running trials and training. The danger is management using it to cut crews, and I wouldn't trust them without the union.
S1.do: Signs up for line robot and drone stringing courses in the first months, even on her own time. Offers to write the district training module and pushes the union for a no-layoff-without-retraining promise.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited at the idea of her hands getting a rest.
S1.quote: I'd teach them to argue with the machine. That's what keeps you alive.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe sees steady disruption as an opening, especially for training. Her trust is in the tools and the union, not management. She immediately thinks of an older colleague who wouldn't adapt and wants him treated fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone and the government needs to step in now: income support, a pause on layoffs, and public control of the grid robots. I'd say it loud, at work and online. I wouldn't be cheering this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd be scrambling. I'd be 60, we'd have two weeks of money, and even if I'm the one who knows the tech, the robot doesn't need a trainer for long. It's the speed that does it, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the first course for robot supervisors that existed, and ask to run the trial crew. We'd cut back hard at home and I'd talk to Dee about closing the café before it eats what little we have. I'd join every union push for a bridge to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake, if that makes sense. Like a storm night: lots to do, no time to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen with the café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. It's Dee's life's work, and I think we'd have to close it or sell it within the year. I don't know how I'd say that to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're usually the one who moves first. Is there anything to move towards here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There'd be a window, maybe a year or two, where someone has to watch the robots, check their work and sign off on safety. I'd want that job. After that I don't know, and I won't pretend I do.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and the government must step in with income support, a pause on layoffs and public control of grid robots. I'd say it loudly at work and online.
S2.think: Privately I'd be scrambling at 60 with two weeks of money. Even knowing the tech, a robot doesn't need a trainer for long, and it's the speed that does it.
S2.do: Signs up for the first robot supervisor course and asks to lead the trial crew. Cuts back hard at home, talks with her wife about closing the café, and joins union pushes for a bridge to retirement.
S2.feel: Anxious but alert, like a storm night with lots to do and no time to panic.
S2.quote: I'd want that job. After that I don't know, and I won't pretend I do.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability keeps her from alarm: she immediately finds a role to aim for, even a short-lived one. The hardest part for her is the café, not her own job. She's honest that her plan only covers a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable if we plan for it now. I'd push the union and our local council to set up a regional transition office, somewhere you can walk in and get advice. I'd be a bit more hopeful in how I said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd land on my feet. Five years puts me at 63, and I could spend most of it training people to work with the robots, then retire. The worry is the money gap at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get qualified on robot supervision early, in the first year, and try to move into a district training role. We'd try to build some savings, even small, and maybe turn the café into something that needs less of us. I'd write to my representative about a public grid robot programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time, but not loads of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a proper certificate in drones and line robots, even if I pay for it myself. Then sit down with Dee and have the café talk while it's a choice, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your kids differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nell, who's 25 and working in a call centre, to start looking now, because those jobs go first. Liam's a plumber, and I'd tell him to learn the robot side of plumbing. I'd tell them both what I tell the apprentices: get good at checking the machine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but workable if we plan now. I'd push the union and council for a regional transition office where people can get advice.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd land on my feet, training people to work with robots until I retire at 63. The worry is the money gap at the end.
S3.do: Gets qualified in robot supervision in the first year and aims for a district training role. Tries to build some savings, rethinks the café with her wife and writes to her representative about a public grid robot programme.
S3.feel: Uneasy, knowing there is time but not much of it.
S3.quote: Have the café talk while it's a choice, not an emergency.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from a scramble into a career shift she can see the end of. She's quick to give practical advice to her children. Her thinking about public programmes fits her progressive outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one we should be aiming for, if we get to choose. Ten years is enough to retrain a whole workforce if someone actually plans it. I'd be pushing hard for that at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'd get to be part of building the new way of working, then retire before it's finished. It's the young apprentices I'd want to look out for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning the robot side now and slowly move into training and safety sign-off over the next few years. I'd help Dee shift the café into something lighter, maybe weekend only. And I'd keep pushing for a proper public plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 then. What does a decade of warning do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do things in order. Train the young ones, pay off a few debts, let Dee wind down the café gently. I'd be retired before it fully arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the work you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The storm nights, oddly. Everyone in the truck at three in the morning, soaked, laughing because the lights just came back on in the whole town. I don't think a robot gets that.

S4.say: I'd say this is the one we should aim for, since ten years is enough to retrain a whole workforce if someone plans it. I'd push hard for that at the union.
S4.think: Privately I think it's good for me: I'd help build the new way of working and retire before it's finished. I'd want to look out for the young apprentices.
S4.do: Starts learning the robot side now and moves into training and safety sign-off over several years. Helps her wife shift the café to weekends and keeps pushing for a public plan.
S4.quote: Everyone in the truck at three in the morning, soaked, laughing because the lights just came back on in the whole town.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's genuinely hopeful and sees a role for herself in building the change. Her plan is orderly: training, debts, the café. The storm-night memory showed what she values beyond the pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I couldn't learn the new kit, but because we've got two weeks of money and Dee's café would have to go. What would help is income support that lets people like me keep training others for a year or two, and a public body that runs the grid robots so the savings stay with us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether the robots will be safe on a live line in a storm. I'd want people like me checking that, not a sales rep. Ask the crews, not just the bosses.

headlineQuote: It's the speed that does it, not the machines.
portrait: Zoe Baker is a 58-year-old storm crew leader and district trainer at a river depot, the person at work who tries every new tool and uses AI every day. Her pay props up her wife Dee's struggling café, which leaves them with about two weeks of savings. She's calm about a plateau or steady change and even sees an opening to make the job safer and teach apprentices to argue with the machine. Fast AGI makes her anxious, mainly because the café would have to close, though she still finds a short-term role to aim for. With five or ten years she sees herself training others, then retiring, and she grows hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because with two weeks of money her wife's café would have to close, even if she could learn the new kit.
whatWouldHelp: Income support so people like her can keep training others for a year or two, and a public body running the grid robots so the savings stay with workers.
